At this point, you should have a solid foundation in Python and programming in
general. We won't be covering the basics here — there are approximately 4.7
million tutorials on loops, conditionals, and functions online, and you should
know this stuff anyway.

What we *will* do is help you graduate from the "I write 300 lines of spaghetti
code in a single script and pray it works" phase to becoming a proper programmer
who knows how to abstract, modularize, and eventually build their own Python
package.

Each section is a **Jupyter notebook** — the code and its output are rendered on
the page, the code blocks are copyable and foldable, and every section ends with
short **self-tests** whose solutions you can reveal.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Run the notebooks yourself
To *run and edit* a section interactively, download its notebook with the
**`</>` Source Code** menu (top-right of each page) and open it in JupyterLab or
VS Code — for example on the [course cluster](../cluster/index.qmd), where the
Python environment is already set up.
:::

## Sections

1. [Efficient scientific plotting](01-plotting.ipynb) — golden rules for
   publication-quality figures, and the Matplotlib code to produce them.
2. [Python foundations](02-foundations.ipynb) — program entry points, data
   structures (comprehensions, `collections`), and file I/O with `pathlib`.
3. [Object-oriented programming](03-oop.ipynb) — classes, properties,
   inheritance, dunder methods, and dataclasses.
4. [Functional programming](04-functional.ipynb) — functions as first-class
   objects, lambdas & `map`, and type hints.
5. [Advanced Python internals](05-internals.ipynb) — decorators, iterators &
   iterables, and generators.
6. [Software engineering practices](06-engineering.ipynb) — validation &
   exceptions, testing, logging, and documentation.
7. [Packaging & distribution](07-packaging.ipynb) — turn your code into an
   installable Python package.

## Package environment

One of the biggest advantages of Python is its rich and well-maintained
ecosystem of packages and libraries. The main downside is that managing these
packages can sometimes become cumbersome, especially when different projects
require different versions.

Python comes with its own package manager, `pip`, which works well —
particularly when used together with **virtual environments**. Another option,
which I personally recommend, is
[Miniforge3](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge). It provides a
lightweight Conda-based environment similar to Anaconda, but without unnecessary
extras, and it uses the `conda-forge` channel by default. This often results in
more reliable and consistent package installations, especially for scientific
computing.

### Required Python packages

For this course, we will mainly rely on the following core scientific Python
packages:

- **NumPy** — efficient array operations, linear algebra, and numerical
  computations.
- **SciPy** — numerical algorithms such as solvers, optimization, integration,
  and interpolation.
- **Matplotlib** — plotting and visualization of results.

Together, these packages form the foundation of the scientific Python ecosystem
and are sufficient for all assignments and projects in this course.

## `.py` vs `.ipynb`

Python code can be written either as plain script files (`.py`) or as Jupyter
notebooks (`.ipynb`). Both formats are useful, but they serve different
purposes.

**`.py` files**

- Best for clean, reproducible code.
- Easy to version control (Git).
- Suitable for larger projects and scripts.
- Less interactive for exploration.

**`.ipynb` files (Jupyter notebooks)**

- Excellent for exploration, learning, and visualization.
- Combine code, text, equations, and plots in one place.
- Very convenient for tutorials and reports.
- Harder to version control cleanly.
- Execution order can be confusing if cells are run out of order.
- Need the extra packages `jupyter` and `ipykernel`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Recommendation
Use Jupyter notebooks for learning, experimentation, and visualization, and
switch to `.py` files once the code becomes larger or more structured.
:::
